notes.meaning: The Sadducees ask Jesus whose wife the woman will be when the dead rise, since all seven brothers had married her on earth. They did not believe in life after death and wanted to make the idea of resurrection look silly. They used Moses' rule about family marriage to argue that bodily resurrection causes impossible problems.

Jesus answers that they are badly mistaken. Their error comes from not understanding what the Scriptures teach and not knowing God's mighty power. God is fully able to raise the dead and create a whole new kind of life.

Jesus explains that earthly marriage will not exist in the resurrection. People will no longer die, so marriage will not be needed to keep the human race going. Resurrected believers will be like the angels in heaven, living forever in deathless bodies.

Jesus answers them from the writings of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted. He reminds them of the story of the burning bush where God spoke to Moses. God told him that He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, long after those patriarchs had died physically.

Jesus explains that God is not the God of dead people, but of the living. Because God keeps His covenant promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, they are still alive with Him in spirit, and their bodies must rise again. The Sadducees were completely wrong about God and the afterlife.

A teacher of the law comes forward after hearing how well Jesus answered the Sadducees. He asks Jesus which commandment is the most important of all. Jewish rabbis often debated which laws in the books of Moses were the greatest and most foundational.

Jesus begins His answer by quoting Deuteronomy, words known as the Shema. He reminds the scribe that the Lord our God is the one and only Lord. True faith begins with knowing the one true God who made us.

Jesus says the greatest command is to love the Lord your God with everything you have. We are called to love Him with our whole heart, soul, mind, and physical strength. This means giving God our deepest feelings, our thoughts, and our daily energy.

Jesus adds a second command that is closely tied to the first: to love your neighbor as yourself. Loving other people comes directly out of loving God. There is no other commandment greater than these two joined together.

The scribe warmly agrees with Jesus and praises His answer as the truth. He repeats that there is only one God and none besides Him. Unlike many other religious leaders, this scribe listened honestly without trying to trap Jesus.

The scribe adds that loving God completely and loving our neighbors matters much more than all animal sacrifices and burnt offerings. Religious rituals outside mean nothing to God without love on the inside. Real love in action is the highest form of worship.

Jesus sees that the scribe spoke with true spiritual understanding and tells him he is not far from God's kingdom. After this exchange, none of the leaders dared to ask Jesus any more trap questions. Understanding God's truth brings a person right to the threshold of faith.

differ.view: The scribe showed genuine spiritual insight and was close to becoming a true follower of Jesus.
Being near the kingdom referred to the arrival of the gospel era, since keeping the law cannot bring anyone into eternal salvation without God's grace.
The law's true role is to reveal our spiritual need, so understanding it brings someone close to seeing their need for Christ.

notes.meaning: While teaching in the temple courtyards, Jesus asks why the scribes claim the Messiah is merely the Son of David. While the Messiah is indeed David's descendant, that title alone does not tell the whole story. Jesus wants the people to see that the promised King is far greater than an earthly ruler.

Jesus quotes Psalm 110, showing that King David spoke under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. In that psalm, God the Father tells David's Lord to sit at His right hand until all enemies are defeated. David clearly recognized that the coming King was his own Master.

Jesus asks how the Messiah can be David's son if David himself calls Him Lord. The answer is that Jesus is both fully human as David's descendant and fully divine as Lord of all. The large crowd listened to Jesus' teaching with great delight.

Jesus warns the crowd and His disciples to watch out for the teachers of religious law. These men loved to walk around in long, flowing robes to show off their importance and enjoyed respectful greetings in public markets. They cared more about getting honor from people than pleasing God.

Jesus points out that these leaders sought out the front seats in the synagogues and the highest places at banquet tables. They loved to be treated as superior to everyone else. Their religion was driven by personal pride rather than humble service.

Behind their holy appearance, these scribes cheated helpless widows out of their property and homes. Then they tried to cover up their greed by saying very long prayers in public. Jesus warns that people who use religion to harm others will face the strictest judgment.

Jesus sits down opposite the temple collection boxes and watches the crowds dropping in their money. Many wealthy people arrived and put in large sums of coins. These voluntary gifts were used to support temple services and daily sacrifices.

A poor widow comes by and drops in two tiny copper coins, worth only a tiny fraction of a day's wage. These coins were the smallest money used at the time. Even though she had almost nothing, she gave what she had to God.

Jesus calls His disciples together to teach them an important truth about giving. He tells them that this penniless widow put in far more than all the rich people. God does not measure gifts by the amount of money, but by the love and sacrifice of the giver.

Jesus explains that the wealthy gave out of their extra money which they did not need, while this widow gave out of extreme poverty. She put in everything she owned and all she had left to live on. Her gift showed complete trust in God to provide for her needs.

differ.view: Rather than praising an example to follow, Jesus is pointing out a tragedy where a corrupt religious system pressured a destitute widow to give up her last bite of food.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teach that Jesus was not praising the widow's gift, but pointing out the tragedy of a greedy religious system that squeezed the very last coins out of poor and vulnerable people.
